title: Bodhana Sivanandan, 11, Earns Third Guinness Title as Youngest Woman Grandmaster
excerpt: Guinness World Records has officially recognised the Indian-origin British prodigy as the youngest chess player ever to earn the Woman Grandmaster title, following her performance at the 2026 Chess Olympiad in Samarkand.
body:
• Guinness World Records has officially recognised 11-year-old Bodhana Sivanandan as the youngest chess player to achieve the Woman Grandmaster (WGM) title — her third Guinness record.
  • She secured the final requirement for the WGM title while representing England on Board 1 at the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan (15–27 September 2026), scoring 8 points from 11 games with a performance rating of 2432.
  • Her two earlier Guinness titles, earned at age 10 — youngest Woman International Master and youngest female player to defeat a grandmaster in a tournament — feature in the new Guinness World Records 2027 book.
  • She also picked up a second International Master (IM) norm at the Olympiad, moving closer to the open IM title, the next rung of her ambitions.

Guinness World Records, the global authority on record-breaking achievements, has officially recognised British chess prodigy Bodhana Sivanandan, 11, as the youngest chess player to achieve the Woman Grandmaster (WGM) title. The recognition, announced this week, follows her history-making performance at the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, where she secured the final requirement for the title and completed one of the most remarkable runs by a junior player in the sport's history.

The new title gives Bodhana three Guinness World Records titles. She has also received her first official Guinness World Records certificates recognising her two earlier achievements, with new photography released to mark the occasion.

A chess career of records

Bodhana's Olympiad campaign was demanding by any standard. Playing all 11 rounds on England's top board — the assignment usually reserved for a team's strongest player — she finished with eight points from 11 games, recording six wins, three draws and two losses for an individual performance rating of 2432. Her score helped England to a 15th-place finish in the women's section, and the event also yielded her second International Master (IM) norm, taking her closer to the open IM title.

The WGM title required three qualifying norms and a rating above the mandatory 2,300 threshold, which she surpassed earlier in 2026, reaching a peak rating of 2,374 in May. In completing it at 11, she shattered the previous age record held by Russia's Kateryna Lagno, who earned the title in 2002 at 12 years and four months. China's Hou Yifan also reached WGM at 12 before becoming the youngest woman to earn the open Grandmaster title.

The two records that preceded this one were both set when Bodhana was just 10: youngest chess Woman International Master, and youngest female player to defeat a grandmaster in a tournament. Both are featured in the newly released Guinness World Records 2027 book — the latest title came after the book had gone to print, so it will have to wait for the 2028 edition.

"It is an absolute honour to be featured in Guinness World Records 2027, which gives me huge encouragement and a real morale boost. It motivates me to keep pushing myself and achieve even more."

— Bodhana Sivanandan

From the 'horsey' piece to chess history

Bodhana's journey into chess began not with dreams of records, but with a fascination for one piece on the board: the knight. She first became interested in the "horsey" piece as a young child and wanted to treat it like any other toy; her father explained that if she took only the knight from the chess set, nobody else would be able to play. She began learning chess at five years and eight months old and started competing at six.

Her rise since has been relentless. She taught herself the rules during the COVID-19 lockdown in 2020 at age five, using a chessboard left behind by a family friend. She swept all 24 games at the 2022 European Schools Championship, became the youngest person to represent England in any international sport in 2024, and in August 2025 became the youngest player to defeat a classical grandmaster, beating French GM Marc'Andria Maurizzi at the Dole Open in France. Earlier in 2026 she became Britain's youngest-ever Women's Chess Champion.

Guinness World Records Editor-in-Chief Craig Glenday said her story showed how a child's curiosity could lead to something extraordinary, adding that what made Bodhana so inspiring was "the joy and determination that she continues to bring to the game." Asked what she would say to another young person who wants to become really good at something they love, Bodhana offered advice as plain as her game is brilliant: "Enjoy what you're doing and keep playing the game you love."

An Indian-origin star lighting up Britain

Bodhana was born and raised in London; her parents hail from Tamil Nadu in India and, remarkably, do not play chess. For the British-Indian community — and the wider Indian diaspora watching from afar — her success carries a particular resonance: a child of Indian heritage, playing under the English flag, beating records set by players from the sport's traditional powerhouses.

Her story also feeds a larger current. India has undergone a chess revolution over the past decade, producing a conveyor belt of teenage grandmasters and the youngest world champion in history, and Bodhana's feats extend that narrative into the diaspora — proof that the culture's passion for the 64 squares travels with it.

What's next

The immediate target is the open International Master title, for which she already holds two norms. In interviews with FIDE she has made clear she remains focused on progressing further and pursuing additional history in open competition rather than simply celebrating the WGM milestone.

For now, though, the certificates tell the story: three Guinness World Records titles before her twelfth birthday, a place in the Guinness World Records 2027 book, and a career trajectory that has chess's sharpest observers reaching for superlatives. The 2028 edition of the book will presumably need a new entry — and Bodhana Sivanandan, by her own account, has no intention of stopping.
nri_angle: Indian-origin British schoolgirl Bodhana Sivanandan, daughter of Tamil Nadu parents, earns her third Guinness World Records title — a point of pride for the British-Indian community and diaspora worldwide.
